---
title: "Methodological flexibility in the use of large language models in research"
---
**Speaker:** Jamie Cummins, University of Bern

### Abstract {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Across the sciences, the ubiquity of generative large language models is difficult to ignore. Researchers have suggested that LLMs can be used to improve and facilitate stages of the research process as diverse as hypothesis generation, study piloting, data analysis, and meta-analysis, to name a few. Others have suggested that LLMs may have interesting (psychological) properties which may be of interest to study in their own right, while others still have suggested that LLMs may even be capable of acting as synthetic research participants to supplement or replace human research participants. These applications are often discussed as though "LLMs" constitute a single method with generalisable properties. This line of thinking, however, is inaccurate: the outputs of LLM-based workflows depend on many interacting analytic choices, and these choices are infrequently considered as a source of variance.

In this talk, I argue that LLM-based workflows should be understood as a topic for meta-science in methods research. Like other methodological pipelines, they are susceptible to selective reporting, asymmetric comparisons, hidden researcher degrees of freedom, and overinterpretation of favorable results. I will present a framework for structuring how and where key methodological choices for LLM workflows arise, and briefly illustrate how small changes to these components can produce markedly different outcomes. I conclude by outlining how practices such as requiring more comprehensive workflow descriptions, sensitivity analysis, and more systematic benchmarking could improve the development and evaluation of LLM-based research.
